An unusually early sudden stratospheric warming event has flipped the polar vortex, leaving analysts worried about rising energy prices.

Europeans brace for what could be a particularly cold winter this year, after an unusually early sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) flipped the polar vortex.

The polar vortex is a ring of westerly winds that keeps freezing polar air locked over the North Pole about 30km above the Earth’s surface.

Sometimes, large atmospheric waves can disrupt this circulation, causing the winds to weaken significantly or even reverse direction. This can cause temperatures in the stratosphere to rise rapidly.

As the cold air from high up in the stratosphere disperses, it can affect the shape of the jet stream as the cold air sinks from the stratosphere into the troposphere, which extends from the ground up to an average altitude of about eight to 15 kilometres.

Europe’s dwindling gas supplies

According to market intelligence provider Montel, forecasters warn that this "heightens the odds of colder temperatures”, more storms, wind and heating demand on the continent over the next month.

However, analysts say this would need to be a “repeated event” to have a sustained effect throughout the winter, as single SSW events are “short-term in nature”.

A severe cold spell could put gas supplies under even more pressure, following warnings from the EU that it may have to curb its gas consumption by seven per cent this winter as stocks hit record lows for this time of year.

Dwindling gas reserves, primarily driven by the war on Iran and subsequent blockade of the Strait of Hormuz – one of the world’s biggest fossil fuel shipping routes – are also set to worsen ahead of a full ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports from January 2027.

The unusually early SSW “might make people a bit nervous”, says Klaas Dozeman, energy forecaster at Brainchild Commodity Intelligence, adding that “most meteorologists remain puzzled on what the effects will be over the coming weeks”.

Can heat pumps save households from spiralling energy bills this winter?

Green technology is cushioning Europe from the ongoing fossil fuel crisis, providing more households with energy security and lower bills.

Solar power, for example, has already saved the EU €44.6 billion in avoided gas imports since the beginning of the US-led war on Iran, which started on 28 February.

But as the days get shorter and darker, it is heat pumps that will offer relief from spiralling energy prices.

Heat pumps, which work by capturing energy from air, water or the ground and turning it into heat or cold air, typically deliver three to four kWh of heat for every one kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity they consume.

Each residential heat pump installed displaces around 1,100 m3 of gas and two tonnes of CO2 per year on average, if the small amount of electricity it uses to run is from renewable sources.

Europe’s heat pumps provide as much heat as the LNG carried by more than 200 tankers, according to an analysis from the European Heat Pump Association published in June*.

This is double the amount that arrived in the EU in 2025 from the Middle East and around seven per cent of the EU’s total annual imported LNG – avoiding €9.7 billion in import costs last year.

“Every heat pump installed is another bolt in the door of European energy security,” says Paul Kenny, director general of EHPA.

“LNG is the most expensive energy source and comes from unreliable suppliers, and heat pumps can drastically reduce our need for it.”

Despite myths suggesting that heat pumps do not work in cold countries, which Euronews Earth has debunked here, new research has found that when used effectively, air source heat pumps could help heat homes on a typical winter day for as little as £1.84 (approximately €2.20) a day.

Heat pumps more efficient than gas boilers

The study, from British property developers Barratt Redrow, found that heat pumps can be more efficient than traditional gas boilers because they keep a more constant temperature rather than relying on spikes of heat.

"Heat pumps will run during the cold but consume a lot more power,” Jean-Paul Harreman, Director at Montel, tells Euronews Earth.

“The efficiency is better from a heat pump than from a gas boiler, but if power prices go really high, high costs might still be seen during the worst of the cold. However, that is usually only part of the winter, so a price spike should not be confused with an annual total cost.”

Heat pump sales rose 13 per cent last year, hitting 2.9 million in 21 European countries. This brings the total stock to 29.3 million.

When asked whether heat pumps could help the EU’s dwindling gas supply, Harreman said: “A little yes. We see electrification of heating happening in many countries, but the overall impact on demand is not that large.

“Industrial demand destruction plays a bigger role.”

Industrial demand destruction is a sustained or permanent drop in industrial consumption of energy caused by prolonged high prices or supply constraints.

*EHPA’s data is based on 21 EU member states. You can read the full analysis here.

From ski slopes to snow-covered mountain towns, these Asian destinations offer an alternative to Europe’s winter resorts.

When it comes to planning a winter getaway, the chances are you might be thinking of heading to Europe's Alpine destinations in France, Switzerland or Austria.

But if you fancy a mid- to long-haul trip away from the continent, Asia has much to offer with snow-covered mountains, ski slopes and a host of resorts worth exploring.

From the landscapes of South Korea, Vietnam, Lebanon and beyond, these destinations deserve a place on your radar for skiing, snowboarding and other winter adventures.

Karakol Ski Resort, Kyrgyzstan

Kyrgyzstan is definitely worth adding to your winter travel bucket list. Picture fresh powder as far as the eyes can see, amid sweeping views of conifer forests.

On the outskirts of Karakol, a Kyrgyz destination for adventure, the Karakol Ski Resort sits at an altitude of 3,040 metres above sea level in the Tian Shan mountain range, which sprawls across the country, as well as China, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. It is also the highest ski resort in Central Asia.

The season usually runs from late November through to April, with the high season being from 31 December to 10 January. During the winter, daytime temperatures rarely drop below -5C, alongside many sunny days.

Aside from the mild climate, there are an array of residences, from hotel rooms to chalet cottages, within the vicinity.

Mzaar Ski Resort, Lebanon

Self-styled as being “above the ordinary”, the Mzaar Ski Resort is perched above the mountain village of Kfardebian and overlooks the breathtaking Lebanese peak, Mount Sannine.

On offer are 115 kilometres of slopes, 19 lifts and a summit at 2,465 metres, making it the largest ski area in the Middle East. Aside from skiing and snowboarding, the winter season is ideal for ziplining over the mountain or riding aboard a snow groomer.

After a long day outdoors, the resort's wellness area is replete with sauna and cold plunge facilities. While there is an outdoor pool, the indoor one is a year-round option for guests to have a swim and unwind.

Accommodation options include the InterContinental Mzaar Mountain Resort & Spa, which has direct access to the 80km Mzaar Ski Domaine, and L’Escale Du Mzaar, which is just 40m from the first chairlift and has chalets and a ski shop.

O2 Ski Resort, South Korea

This resort in South Korea offers speedy rides 1,420 metres above sea level.

Located in the city of Taebaek, O2 Ski Resort has 16 slopes and six lifts, including one which goes up to the top of Hambaek Mountain, where visitors can take in sweeping views.

Facilities include an extreme park, half pipe and a 136m-long snow sledge, with snow made from Han and Nakdong river sources.

Via the gondola, visitors can head to the resting spot at the highest peak, Eutteum Maru, which overlooks the Baekdu mountain range. Beogeum Maru also offers skiers a place to rest, and is easily accessible to novice visitors as it sits between the beginners' slopes.

Sapa, Vietnam

While Southeast Asia isn’t famed for its snowy landscapes, you should also add Vietnam to your winter must-visit lists.

When the temperature drops over the Hoàng Liên Sơn mountain range – the country's highest peaks – frost and the occasional dusting settle over rice terraces.

In Sapa, the town can transform into a snowy sight from December to late January – occasionally extending into early February. During this time, the air becomes crisp, the mountains become capped by snow and the waterfalls also freeze over.

Vietnam Airlines recommends travellers to add Fansipan Mountain to their Sapa itineraries, which stands at 3,143 metres. The country's highest snow-capped peak is accessible via the Sun World Fansipan Legend cable car.

The carrier also suggests paying Bát Xát Commune a visit, as it receives some of Sapa's heaviest snowfall during the winter. The remote retreat's rice terraces and forests become pearly white landscapes during this time.

Meanwhile, Thác Bạc, or the Silver Waterfall, which is on the outskirts of Sapa, is a 200-metre cascade that frequently freezes.

Shahdag Mountain Resort, Azerbaijan

On the outskirts of Gusar city in Azerbaijan’s Greater Caucasus mountain range, the Shahdag Mountain Resort takes its name from Mount Shahdag, which stands 4,243 metres above sea level. This ski and snowboarding playground features 45 kilometres of pristine terrain, including a selection of 37 slopes and a network of 20 lifts.

Winter paintballing, mountain trekking, snow tubing as well as horseback riding are some of the other activities on offer at the resort during the winter. Visitors are also spoiled for choice when it comes to dining with more than 20 venues among five hotels.

At the backdrop of all this are pristine glaciers, deep ravines, stunning canyons and a variety of flora, fauna and wildlife.

Shymbulak Mountain Resort, Kazakhstan

The Shymbulak Mountain Resort is located in the gorge of Trans-Ili Alatau, within the city limits of Kazakhstan's cultural hub, Almaty. The resort itself sits at an elevation ranging from 2,200 metres to 3,180 metres above sea level.

With a total of 10 lifts, adventure travellers are treated to slopes with a total length of up to 20 kilometres and elevation difference of up to 920 metres for both beginners and experts.

The resort features a range of accommodation options, including the Nero Bianca high mountain chalets, which features its own sauna.

Meanwhile, the Le Mont boutique hotel welcomes guests, including those with four-legged companions. It has a viewing platform, with the panorama of Almaty and snow-capped peaks on display. Other options include Shymbulak Resort Hotel and Tenir Eco Hotels.

Zao Onsen Ski Resort, Japan

The Zao Onsen Ski Resort in Yamagata sits amid mountains and vast wilderness, offering a winter playground where the longest run is more than 10 kilometres long.

The Japanese resort features 32 lifts, ropeways and a gondola that goes up to the 1,661-metre summit station. Experienced skiers can enjoy ski jumps, while there are also routes that run through forests for skiers and snowboarders alike.

At the top lifts, keep an eye out for what the locals call "Juhyo", or snow monsters, that the area is known for during the peak of winter in February.

A combination of Siberian winds and heavy snowfall turn the Alpine trees into giant, monster-like figures. There's even a Zao Snow Monster festival where snow monster mascots entertain visitors.

Soil degradation could cost the EU between €286 billion and €509 billion over its next long-term budget if losses stay at current levels, campaign group Save Soil estimates, urging the bloc to pay farmers for measurable gains in soil health through its next farm subsidy scheme.

Damaged soils could drain €286 billion to €509 billion from the EU economy over the bloc's 2028 to 2034 budget if yearly losses continue at today's pace, Save Soil estimated on Thursday.

The global campaign group wants the next Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the EU's farm subsidy system, to reward farmers for proven gains in soil health instead of leaving them to bear the cost of restoration.

Save Soil was launched in 2022 by Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru and his non-profit Isha Foundation to push governments into adopting policies that protect and restore soils.

Its estimate builds on research by the European Commission's in-house science service, the Joint Research Centre (JRC), which puts the yearly cost of soil degradation in the EU at €40.9 billion to €72.7 billion.

Save Soil multiplied that by the seven years of the next long-term budget currently being discussed in Brussels.

The range covers erosion, contamination, compaction and soil carbon losses, among other damage, and the JRC has noted the bill could double if costs such as biodiversity loss, floods, droughts and health effects were added.

Farm budget talks

In July 2025, the Commission proposed ring-fencing at least €300 billion for farmers' income and crisis support from 2028. On 26 October, EU agriculture ministers agreed their stance on the CAP rules but left funding to the wider budget talks.

Agriculture negotiations at COP31 in Türkiye, ended without a meaningful outcome, with a decision pushed back to 2027.

"Europe is debating hundreds of billions in agricultural support while soil degradation is already imposing enormous costs on its economy," Rico Rau, the lead author of the group's COP31 report, said in a statement.

"The next CAP should not simply compensate farmers for the pressures they face. It should help them rebuild the productive asset their livelihoods depend on," he added.

Risks to the food industry

According to the Commission, 60% to 70% of soils in the EU are unhealthy, weakening their ability to support farming, hold water and cope with extreme weather.

Poorer soils can cut yields, raise costs and make supply chains more fragile, Save Soil warned. The EU's food and drink sector alone turns over €1.5 trillion a year and employs 4.8 million people, according to industry body FoodDrinkEurope.

Save Soil wants the CAP to pay for measurable soil health gains and to reward farmers whose land is already healthy.

It also called for the Soil Monitoring Law, the EU's first soil law, to provide consistent evidence without duplicating measurements and paperwork. The law took effect in December 2025 but sets no binding restoration targets.

Its other two proposals are for the EU's carbon farming certification scheme to reward verified environmental benefits, and for public bodies to use their buying power to secure steady demand for sustainably grown food.

"If we want to ensure food security, farming has to be lucrative," Sadhguru stated in comments shared by the group, adding that governments must make farming profitable or farmers’ children will not take it up.

Five EU countries have agreed to a deal with Rwanda to send rejected asylum seekers there from 2027. The agreement is enabled by the EU's new return regulation, which stipulates that such deals can only be made with countries that respect human rights. Does Rwanda meet that standard?

Five EU countries have unveiled this week a deal to deport rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece will kick off this plan in 2027, with around 100 single men who cannot be deported directly to their home countries being sent to Rwanda.

The agreement is enabled by the EU return regulation, which entered into force last month. This marks the first time a group of EU member states have used the framework to send irregular migrants to a so-called “return hub.”

Article 14 of this law says that deals to deport migrants can only be made with countries that respect human rights, and many have expressed doubts about whether that is the case for Rwanda.

Freedom House, a US-based organisation which measures freedom around the world, gives the country a score of 7 points out of 40 in political rights and 14 out of 60 in civil liberties. Overall, they label Rwanda as “not free.”

The country also received a score of 0 out of 4 on judicial independence, raising questions about whether migrants not receiving proper treatment in Rwanda would be able to challenge their situation in court freely.

The United Nations Human Rights Council has also said this year that Rwandan authorities “suppress opposition and dissent, prosecuting political opponents, journalists and human rights defenders.”

Meanwhile, Amnesty International notes that Rwanda may be implicated in war crimes because of its support of M23, an armed group in the Democratic Republic of the Congo that is allegedly responsible for summary killings and gang rape. War crimes are amongst the worst possible human rights violations.

The EU Parliament itself has proposed to suspend agreements with Rwanda because of these allegations.

Opponents also point to a precedent: a deal between the UK and Rwanda to send people there while their asylum requests were being processed (so not the same as the EU-Rwanda deal, but similar) was blocked by the UK Supreme Court because it found a real risk that Rwanda would send refugees back to the countries they had fled, which is forbidden by international law.

Rwanda’s government has pushed back and says that human rights are respected in the country and that an independent monitoring mechanism, to which the 5 EU countries have committed, will ensure that.

The parties also say that the UN Refugee Agency will have a role in making sure human rights are protected.
